context_blurb:
Watch the Moon for a month and you will see it change: a thin curved sliver, then a half circle, then a bright round disc, and back again. These shapes are the Moon's phases, and the same line-ups of Sun, Moon and Earth that make them also make eclipses.

The Sun always lights one half of the Moon, the half facing it. As the Moon travels round Earth, a bigger or smaller part of its sunlit half faces Earth, and that changing slice is the phase. Many people think Earth's shadow makes the phases, but it does not: Earth's shadow touches the Moon only during a lunar eclipse. In a room lit by one lamp, hold a ball at arm's length a little above your head and turn slowly round: you will see crescent, half and full, though your shadow never touches the ball.

At new moon the Moon lies between the Sun and Earth. Its sunlit half faces away from us, so the side we see is dark, and the Moon is lost in the daytime glare near the Sun. Just then the Moon's far side is lit all over by the Sun. People often call the far side the dark side, but it gets just as much sunlight as the near side.

From new moon the lit part grows, and a growing Moon is waxing. First comes a thin waxing crescent, less than half lit; then first quarter, a half circle; then the waxing gibbous Moon, more than half lit; and about two weeks after new moon, the full moon. After full moon the lit part shrinks, and a shrinking Moon is waning: it passes through waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent, and so back to new moon.

At full moon the Moon is on Earth's far side from the Sun, so its whole sunlit half faces us. That is why a full moon rises at sunset and stays up all night: as the spinning Earth turns your home away from the Sun in the evening, it turns you toward the Moon. The Moon takes about 27 days to go once round Earth, and in that same time it turns once on its own axis. Because it spins once for each trip round Earth, it always keeps the same face toward us. Walk once round a chair while facing it, and you turn round once yourself without ever showing it your back.

In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light from part of Earth, and it can do that only when it stands between the Sun and Earth, which happens at new moon alone. The Sun's width is some 400 times the Moon's, but the Sun also lies about 400 times farther away, so the two look about the same size in our sky. A coin held close to your eye can hide a distant house the same way. By the time it reaches Earth, the Moon's darkest shadow has narrowed to a strip rarely more than a few hundred kilometres wide, and only inside it is the Sun fully hidden.

Still, most months pass with no eclipse at all. The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees to Earth's path round the Sun, so at most new moons the Moon slides just above or below the Sun, and its shadow misses Earth. Only when a new moon falls where the two paths cross does an eclipse happen, a few times a year. A Moon farther away than usual still makes an eclipse, leaving a bright ring of Sun round its edge.

A lunar eclipse is the other way round. Earth's shadow points straight away from the Sun, and the Moon can drift into it only at full moon, when it sits beyond Earth with its whole sunlit face turned toward us. At every other phase the Moon passes off to one side of the shadow. When the whole Moon is inside, it does not disappear but turns a deep coppery red: a blood moon. Earth's air bends some sunlight round the edge of the planet and into the shadow, and on the way the air scatters away most of the blue light, the same reason sunsets look red. So the red glow is sunlight bent through Earth's air. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is safe to watch with bare eyes.
